hints: Think about what happens to the C=C double bond when propene joins a chain, and how the two carbons link to neighbours.
For the diacid plus diol, focus on which OH groups combine to split out a small molecule at each ester link.
Count how many ester links form per pair of monomers to work out how many water molecules are released.
walkthrough:
Build the addition repeat unit from propene**
Picture $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_3$. In addition polymerisation the pi bond opens and each monomer adds by two new single bonds to neighbours. So you get a saturated carbon chain: $-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-$. Keep the $\text{CH}_3$ side chain untouched, that is the fingerprint of polypropene.

Build the polyester repeat unit**
Now you have a dicarboxylic acid $\text{HOOC-CH}_2\text{-COOH}$ and a diol $\text{HO-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-OH}$. Each $\text{COOH} + \text{OH}$ pair forms an ester link $-\text{COO}-$ plus water. Joining them alternately gives $-[\text{CO-CH}_2\text{-CO-O-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-O}]-$ as one repeat unit.

Add the small molecule**
Addition polymerisation gives no other product. Condensation polymerisation always eliminates a small molecule. Here two ester bonds form per repeat unit, so $2n\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is released overall, written as $+ \text{H}_2\text{O}$ per ester link.

Final answer: Addition: $n\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_3(g) \rightarrow -[\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)]_n-$
Condensation: $n\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H} + n\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \rightarrow -[\text{COCH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{O}]_n- + 2n\text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: Compare the number of free particles before and after when n gas monomers become one polymer chain.
Consider what extra product appears in condensation polymerisation and how that changes the total number of molecules.
walkthrough:
Link entropy to freedom of movement**
Remember entropy measures disorder. Gases are highly disordered with particles moving freely. A solid polymer chain holds atoms in fixed positions, much more ordered.

Apply to addition**
You start with $n$ moles of gaseous $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_3$ flying around independently and end with essentially one large molecule. Far fewer ways to arrange the particles, so disorder falls sharply. That means $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ is negative.

Apply to condensation**
Here monomers also join, which alone would lower entropy. But each joining also frees $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules. Those extra small, mobile molecules add many new ways to distribute energy, so overall disorder increases. That makes $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ likely positive.

Final answer: $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ for addition polymerisation is negative because many disordered gas molecules combine into one ordered chain, decreasing disorder.
$\Delta S^{\ominus}$ for condensation polymerisation is likely positive because small $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules are released alongside the polymer, increasing total number of molecules and disorder.

hints: Focus on joining the carbonyl carbon to the amine nitrogen and spotting the small molecule lost in any acid plus alcohol or amine condensation.
walkthrough:
Join acid to amine with loss of water**
Line up $\text{R-C(=O)-OH}$ with $\text{H}_2\text{N-R}'$. The $\text{OH}$ from the acid and one $\text{H}$ from the amine leave as $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, leaving $\text{R-C(=O)-NH-R}'$, which is the amide $\text{RCONHR}'$.
Final answer: $\text{R-CO}_2\text{H} + \text{H}_2\text{N-R}' \rightarrow \text{RCONHR}' + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: List all bonds in the reactants that disappear when the C-OH group becomes C-N in the amide.
Look at the new amide link and the new water molecule to see which two bonds did not exist before.
walkthrough:
Spot what must break**
To turn $\text{R-C-OH}$ into $\text{R-C-N}$, the $\text{C-O}$ bond in the acid must snap. To free an $\text{H}$ for water, one $\text{N-H}$ bond in the amine must also snap. The $\text{C=O}$ stays intact throughout.

Spot what must make**
The fragments rejoin in two places. Carbon joins nitrogen to give the new amide $\text{C-N}$ bond. The $\text{OH}$ fragment joins $\text{H}$ to give the new $\text{O-H}$ bond in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (the second $\text{O-H}$ was already present in the acid).

Final answer: Bonds broken: $\text{C-O}$ and $\text{N-H}$
Bonds formed: $\text{C-N}$ and $\text{O-H}$

hints: Recall the bond enthalpy expression $\Delta H = \sum$(broken) $- \sum$(formed) and identify the values to sum for each side.
Check the Data Booklet values for $\text{C-O}$, $\text{N-H}$, $\text{C-N}$ and $\text{O-H}$ and keep track of exothermic sign.
walkthrough:
Sum bonds broken**
Breaking is endothermic. Using Data Booklet values: $\text{C-O}$ is $360$ and $\text{N-H}$ is $390$, both in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Total in $= 360 + 390 = 750\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Sum bonds formed and subtract**
Forming is exothermic. $\text{C-N}$ is $305$ and $\text{O-H}$ is $460$. Total out $= 305 + 460 = 765\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Then $$\Delta H^{\ominus} = \sum \text{broken} - \sum \text{formed} = 750 - 765 = -15\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Slightly exothermic, as forming slightly stronger bonds outweighs breaking.

Final answer: Energy absorbed to break bonds $= 360 + 390 = 750\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
Energy released on forming bonds $= 305 + 460 = 765\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
$$\Delta H^{\ominus} = 750 - 765 = -15\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

hints: Start from the Gibbs equation $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ and set the boundary for feasibility.
Rearrange for $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ at $\Delta G^{\ominus} = 0$ and watch the units of $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ in kJ versus J.
walkthrough:
Set the spontaneity boundary**
A reaction is feasible when $\Delta G^{\ominus} \le 0$. The minimum (most negative) $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ still allowed occurs at the limit $\Delta G^{\ominus} = 0$. From $$\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$$ this gives $0 = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$, so $\Delta S^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus}/T$.

Substitute with correct units**
Convert $\Delta H^{\ominus} = -6.00\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ to $-6000\text{ J mol}^{-1}$ because entropy is required in $\text{J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$. Then $$\Delta S^{\ominus} = -6000/298 = -20.1\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$$ Any value more positive than this gives negative $\Delta G$ at $298\text{ K}$.

Final answer: At feasibility limit $\Delta G^{\ominus} = 0$, so $\Delta H^{\ominus} = T\Delta S^{\ominus}$
$$\Delta S^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus}/T = -6000/298 = -20.1\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$$

hints: Recognise the change from two $\text{CH}_3$ side chains to two $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups as a strong oxidation of the benzylic carbon.
walkthrough:
Identify vigorous side chain oxidation**
Both methyl groups on 1,4-dimethylbenzene are oxidised right up to carboxylic acids while the benzene ring survives. That needs a powerful hot oxidiser, concentrated $\text{KMnO}_4$ with heating under reflux.
Final answer: Heat with concentrated $\text{KMnO}_4$ (acidified, followed by acidification if alkaline conditions used).

hints: Identify reaction 2 as reduction of two $\text{NO}_2$ groups to two $\text{NH}_2$ groups, which needs a reducing metal in acid.
Remember what happens to the amine product in strong acid and how the free amine is released.
walkthrough:
Reduce nitro to amine**
Changing $\text{O}_2\text{N-}$ to $\text{H}_2\text{N-}$ is a six electron reduction per group. The classic laboratory system is tin metal with concentrated hydrochloric acid, heated.

Release the free diamine**
In strong acid the product exists as the $\text{-NH}_3^+$ salt. Adding excess $\text{NaOH}$ deprotonates it to give the free 1,4-diaminobenzene.
Final answer: $\text{Sn}$ and concentrated $\text{HCl}$, heat under reflux, then add $\text{NaOH}$ (to liberate free amine from $\text{-NH}_3^+$ salt).

hints: Look at the amide $\text{N-H}$ and $\text{C=O}$ groups in neighbouring Kevlar chains and recall the strongest intermolecular force they can form.
Consider what force can operate between the flat benzene rings stacked close together in aligned chains.
walkthrough:
Hydrogen bonds lock chains together**
Kevlar chains line up side by side. The polar $\text{N-H}$ on one chain points directly at the polar $\text{C=O}$ on the next chain. This $\text{N-H}...\text{O=C}$ hydrogen bond is strong and highly directional, giving great tensile strength and rigidity.

Aromatic stacking adds further attraction**
The repeat unit contains three para linked benzene rings. When chains pack closely, the large electron clouds of these rings induce temporary dipoles in neighbours, creating extensive London dispersion forces that further resist slipping and bending.

Final answer: Hydrogen bonding between $\text{N-H}$ (donor) and $\text{C=O}$ (acceptor) of amide groups on adjacent chains.
Induced dipole-dipole (London dispersion / van der Waals) forces between benzene rings.
